                                 JORDAN JAFFE’S REPLY BRIEF

        Jordan Jaffe timely submits this Reply Brief in support of Route 894, the Applicants’

Proposed Route, and in response to the initial briefs filed by other parties to this proceeding, and

would respectfully show as follows:


                                  I.      EXECUTIVE SUMMARY


        The Initial Briefs filed by other parties do not disturb the case for Route 894. The parties

agree that route selection is a holistic balancing of the Commission’s routing factors, in which no

single factor controls or is dispositive.1 On that holistic analysis, Route 894 achieves the best

overall balance of any route in this record. Parties advancing competing routes can point to

strengths on individual criteria, but none matches Route 894’s combination of low cost, strong

 route-wide paralleling, low habitable-structure impacts, and limited park proximity—or its

avoidance of the Cavallino Airport conflict that the routes relying on Link J33 share. 2

        That balance is evident across the factors the parties dispute. Route 894 avoids the

Cavallino Airport conflict3—an additional, FAA-recognized private-airstrip conflict that the

Environmental Assessment (“EA”) never studied and that no party’s Initial Brief, including the

Applicants’, contests.4 It places among the fewest habitable structures within 500 feet of centerline

of any filed route,5 and it avoids the more sensitive occupied structures, such as the Florence

Elementary School, found along competing alignments.6 It is less expensive than nearly every

competing route advanced by other parties,7 and the few that cost marginally less do not outweigh

its stronger performance on the remaining factors.8 Measured route-wide, as the rule directs, it

parallels compatible right-of-way (“ROW”) in the upper tier of all filed routes. 9 Lastly, Route 894

minimizes the impacts to Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks. 10

        The Commission’s routing criteria exist to identify the route that distributes the burden of

a major transmission line in the least intrusive manner the project’s engineering and cost

      The evidence supports using the Joint Applicants’ Proposed Route 894.

              o Cavallino Airport – The Joint Applicants did not contest Link J33’s negative

                failing to meet the burden of proof that the link is viable. Avoiding Link J33 would
                avoid these potential safety hazards.
              o Habitable Structures – The Joint Applicants’ Proposed Route not only impacts
                fewer habitable structures overall, such as those concentrated along Links E6 and

                Elementary School on Link F34.
              o Cost – The Joint Applicants’ Proposed Route is significantly less expensive than
                almost every other route presented in Initial Brief.
              o Paralleling – Many of those Initial Briefs that oppose the Joint Applicants’
                Proposed Route on the basis of property paralleling and fragmentation only concern

              o Parks – Staten Creek Ranch’s state-park objection does not disqualify Route 894.

                                         II.     INTRODUCTION


       As set out in Mr. Jaffe’s Initial Brief and the testimony of former PUCT Chairman Arthur

D’Andrea, the Joint Applicants’ Route 894 achieves the best overall balance across the

Commission’s routing criteria,12 and the Initial Briefs filed by other parties do not alter that

conclusion. Route 894 avoids the Cavallino Airport conflict shared by every Link J33 route, places

among the fewest habitable structures of any filed route while avoiding the most sensitive ones, is

less expensive than nearly every competing route, parallels compatible ROW route-wide in the

upper tier of all filed routes, and minimizes impacts to the Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge

State Parks.


       11
            16 TAC § 25.101(B); PURA § 37.056.
       12
            Jaffe Ex. 1, Direct Testimony of Arthur D’Andrea at 15:17-19.
         The competing routes supported by other parties are worth considering but do not

overcome these advantages. Nor do those briefs address the Cavallino Airport conflict that the EA

omitted and is an issue for all the routes built on Link J33. Considered on the full record, the

comparison favors Route 894, and the PUCT should select Route 894.


 III.        THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS USING THE JOINT APPLICANTS’ PROPOSED

                                                     ROUTE 894


              A. The Joint Applicants did not contest Link J33’s negative impacts to Cavallino
                 Airport in either their rebuttal testimony or initial brief, thus failing to meet the
                 burden of proof that the link is viable. Avoiding Link J33 would avoid these
                 potential safety hazards.

        None of the initial briefs, including the Joint Applicants’, address or contest the existence

of the Cavallino Airport, its FAA recognition, its proximity to Link J33, or the safety risks and

operational impact of Link J33 on the Airport. 13 Mr. D’Andrea’s analysis of the conflict therefore

stands uncontroverted. As he explained in his direct testimony, because the EA never identified

the Airport despite its location well within the 10,000-foot radius the EA itself used to inventory

airstrips, every route that includes Link J33 must be treated as carrying one additional private-

airstrip conflict beyond what the Application and EA report. 14 That omission renders the EA’s

analysis of Link J33 materially incomplete, such that Joint Applicants have failed to establish that

the link—or any route utilizing it—is viable, as required by statute and Commission rule. 15 As

one of the first 765-kV transmission line applications to ever be reviewed and potentially approved

 by the PUCT, this case is particularly consequential. Joint Applicants must be held to the long-

established burden of proof to establish, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the application

addresses all statutory and regulatory criteria and that requested route “to the extent reasonable

moderate[s] the impact on the affected community and landowners.” 16 Where an applicant fails

to meet that burden of proof, as Joint Applicants fail to do here with all routes utilizing Link J33,

the Commission can and must partially approve, modify, or reject that route outright. 17

        Route 894 does not use Link J33 and avoids the Cavallino Airport conflict entirely. 18 That

distinction carries practical weight beyond the routing comparison. The Joint Applicants have

deferred all FAA coordination to the post-approval phase, committing only to consult with the

FAA and follow any resulting requirements after the PUCT selects a route. 19 As a result, this

record contains no assessment of whether a 765-kV line on Link J33 can be built and operated

consistent with the Airport’s safe use. Selecting a route that includes Link J33 would therefore

commit the PUCT to a route whose conflict with an FAA-recognized airport has not been studied

in this record and would be examined, if at all, only after approval—with no present assurance

about the limitations the line might impose on the Airport’s operations. 20 Route 894 presents no

such conflict and no such uncertainty.21 Where a route avoids a known conflict that the routes

those routes, the Commission should prefer the route that avoids it. 22

         Although intervenors’ Initial Briefs also fail to address the Cavallino Airport, some oppose

Route 894 on the grounds that other routes impact slightly fewer airports. 23 However, these briefs

fail to consider the qualitative impacts to airports. As discussed in Mr. Jaffe’s Initial Brief, the

Cavallino Airport features a 4,500-foot runway, which is being expanded to approximately 5,400

feet to accommodate larger aircraft, located only approximately 5,600 feet from the centerline of

proposed Link J33.24 A 765-kV transmission line of the height contemplated in the Application,

placed this close to the runway, raises the kind of aviation-safety and obstruction concern that the

FAA’s airspace-protection rules are designed to address: it threatens the approach and departure

corridors on which pilots rely and would constrain the categories of aircraft the Airport is designed

to accommodate, both now and as it expands. 25 Due to the size of aircraft and air traffic volume

at Cavallino Airport, these safety concerns are qualitatively greater than those for a small, private,

recreational airstrip.

               B. The Joint Applicants’ Proposed Route not only impacts fewer habitable structures
                  overall, such as those concentrated along Links E6 and E12, but also avoids
                  particularly sensitive structures such as the Florence Elementary School on Link
                  F34.

         Although other parties such as Aaron Games oppose Route 894 due to its impact on

habitable structures,26 Route 894 ranks among the very fewest habitable structures of any filed

alignments.27 Prudent avoidance is a particularly significant criterion here given the wide disparity

among the filed routes: the number of habitable structures within 500 feet of centerline ranges

from 80 to 184 across the 122 filed routes.28 Route 894 sits near the bottom of that range, with

only 85 habitable structures within 500 feet of its centerline—well below the midpoint and among

the lowest of any filed route.29

         Beyond the raw count, Route 894 avoids structures of heightened sensitivity. Certain routes

concentrate residences along particular links—for example, the residential concentrations along

Links E6 and E1230—and route directly past especially sensitive uses such as the Florence

Elementary School on Link F34. 31 Route 894 avoids these structures. To the extent other parties

contend that habitable-structure impacts should not be treated identically across structure types,

this point favors Route 894: it not only minimizes the overall count but also steers clear of the

most sensitive occupied structures along the competing alignments.

               C. The Joint Applicants’ Proposed Route is significantly less expensive than almost
                  every other route presented in Initial Briefs.

Shanklin Trust,32 oppose Route 894 on the basis of cost, Route 894 is less expensive compared to

price alone where Route 894 performs better across the remaining statutory factors. 33 Route 894

carries an estimated total cost of approximately $1.681 billion—only about 2.73% more than the

least costly of the 122 filed routes and roughly 9.52% less than the most expensive. 34 It is also less

expensive than nearly every competing route advanced by other parties. 35 The Northern Corridor

routes that Staten Creek Ranch champions cost more than Route 894 36 (Route 392 at $1.715 billion

and Route 410 at $1.737 billion), as does the Southern Corridor’s Route 296 ($1.685 billion) and

Route CCG ($1.755 billion).37

        Where a competing route is marginally cheaper than Route 894, the differential is

immaterial. The PUCT is not obligated to select the single lowest-cost route, and modest cost

differences are routinely justified when a route performs better on the other statutory factors. 38

Here, Route 894’s slight premium over the few cheaper alternatives is more than offset by its

superior performance on length, prudent avoidance, and paralleling, and by its avoidance of the

Cavallino Airport conflict.39 To the extent any party argues that cost alone favors its preferred

               D. Many of those Initial Briefs that oppose the Joint Applicants’ Proposed Route on
                  the basis of property paralleling and fragmentation only concern specific
                  individual properties, rather than considering the Route’s positive performance on
                  paralleling across its entire length.

         Some parties object to Route 894 on paralleling or fragmentation grounds. 41 Those

objections, however, are often framed around the effect of the line on specific individual properties

rather than the route’s performance across its full length. The PUCT’s rule directs a route-wide

inquiry: it prefers routes that parallel or utilize existing compatible ROW—including existing

transmission lines, public roads and highways, railroads, and apparent property lines—over the

route as a whole.42

         On that measure, Route 894 parallels existing compatible ROW or apparent property

boundaries for approximately 43.9% of its length, placing it in the upper tier of all 122 filed

routes.43 A complaint that the line does not parallel an existing feature across one party’s particular

tract does not undermine that route-wide performance; nearly every route will diverge from some

compatible corridor at some point along a line spanning more than 200 miles. The relevant

comparison is holistic, and Route 894 performs well on it.

               E. E. Staten Creek Ranch’s state-park objection does not disqualify Route 894.

        Staten Creek Ranch’s objection that Mr. Jaffe’s witness, Mr. D’Andrea, did not consider

the impact to parks does not disqualify Route 894. Staten Creek Ranch urges the PUCT to reject

every Central Corridor route—including Route 894—on the theory that those routes cause

avoidable impacts to Colorado Bend and Post Oak Ridge State Parks. 44 Staten Creek Ranch

criticizes Mr. D’Andrea, among other witnesses, for relying on the routing factors the EA applied

uniformly across all 122 filed routes rather than separately analyzing the two parks. Commission

Staff, however, explicitly weighed park proximity and still recommended a Central Corridor route,

Route 487,45 acknowledging that aesthetic values “would be negatively impacted by any of the

proposed routes.”46 A route’s proximity to a park, while worthy of consideration, cannot be the

disqualifying defect that Staten Creek describes it to be. The applicable inquiry remains the

comparative balancing PURA requires, in which “no one factor controls or is dispositive.” 47

        On that comparison, Route 894 impacts the two parks markedly less than Staff’s own Route

487. Route 894’s Colorado River crossing on Segments J22-J23-J27 stays roughly 0.61 to 1.0

mile from both parks, registers zero parks within 1,000 feet, and places no ROW within the

foreground visual zone of any park.48 Route 487, by contrast, uses Segment J11 which Staten

Creek notes abuts Colorado Bend at roughly 100 feet, crosses the park’s main entrance, and which

         Furthermore, the Northern Corridor routes Staten Creek prefers are more expensive than

Route 894 and burden more residences (Route 392 adds roughly $34.3 million and 51 habitable

structures within 500 feet; Route 410 roughly $56.5 million and 13 habitable structures within 500

feet).52 The balance PURA requires favors Route 894.


                                              IV.      CONCLUSION


         Route 894 achieves the best overall balance across the applicable PURA and PUCT routing

criteria: it is near the shortest and least expensive of the filed routes, parallels compatible existing

ROW for nearly 44% of its length, places among the fewest habitable structures near its centerline,

and impacts the two state parks the least of any route of interest. 53 It also avoids the Cavallino

Airport conflict shared by every Link J33 route—a conflict that no parties’ initial brief contests

and the EA never studied. 54 Nothing in the competing initial briefs overcomes those advantages.
